title: Esther Names Her Enemy
overview: At her second banquet Esther reveals the plot against her people, names Haman as its author, and Haman is executed on the pole he built for Mordecai.

parts.label: The king asks again (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: At the second banquet the king repeats his offer of up to half the kingdom, a formal way of promising great generosity. He has now asked three times, which gives Esther her opening.

parts.label: Esther pleads for her life (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: Esther reveals she belongs to the people marked for death, using three words for total destruction that echo Haman's decree. She adds that she would have stayed silent over mere slavery, though the Hebrew at the end of verse 4 is unclear and translations differ.

parts.label: The king demands a name (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: The king is outraged that anyone would plot this, even though he had approved Haman's decree without asking who it targeted. Esther points straight at Haman, who is sitting at the table with them.

parts.label: Haman begs and seals his fate (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: The king storms into the garden, and Haman stays to beg Esther for mercy, falling onto the couch where she reclined to eat. The returning king treats this as an assault on the queen, and Haman's face is covered, likely a sign that he was condemned.

parts.label: Haman's own pole (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: One of the king's attendants points out the pole, about 75 feet (23 meters) high, that Haman had raised to execute Mordecai, the man who had once saved the king's life. Haman dies on it; translations differ on whether this was hanging or impaling, and impaling was a known Persian punishment.

disagreement: Because God is never named in Esther, Christians differ on how strongly to read Haman's downfall as God quietly at work behind events, rather than simply as the story's sharp reversal of fortune.
think: When someone falls into the very trap they set for others, does that feel like justice to you, or like something else?
